title: Advanced Tenses
tagline: Year 2 — Perfect and continuous forms, conditionals, reported speech and "wish" sentences

introduction.overview: Year 1 covered the twelve tenses and their basic use. Year 2 deals with how tenses work together in a sentence: sequence of tenses, conditionals (if-sentences), reported speech, sentences with wish, "it is high time" and "would rather", and structures such as hardly…when and no sooner…than. These patterns are the favourite targets of fill-in-the-blank and error-spotting questions.
introduction.placementRelevance: Advanced tense and conditional questions are commonly asked in the verbal ability section of company aptitude rounds, in fill-in-the-blank and error-spotting formats.
introduction.realWorldContext: Reports, minutes of meetings and emails depend on correct tenses in reported speech and in conditional statements ("if we had started earlier, we would have finished").

learningObjectives: Use all three types of conditional sentences correctly
Change direct speech into reported speech with correct tense shifts
Use wish, would rather, it is high time and as if correctly
Use past perfect and future perfect forms for sequence and completion

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: Perfect = has/have/had + V3. Continuous = be + V-ing. Perfect continuous = has/have/had been + V-ing. Time words guide the choice (since, for, by the time, before).

coreDefinitions: Conditional type 1 (real future): If + present, will + base verb. Type 2 (unreal present): If + past, would + base verb. Type 3 (unreal past): If + past perfect, would have + V3.
Reported speech: the speaker's words reported by someone else; verbs usually move one tense back after a past reporting verb.
Sequence of tenses: the tense of the subordinate clause is linked to the tense of the main clause.
Subjunctive: the base form used after verbs like suggest, insist, demand ("He suggested that she see a doctor").
Inversion with hardly/scarcely/no sooner: "Hardly had he reached when…", "No sooner had she left than…".
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: English tenses express not only time but also reality. The simple past in "If I were rich" does not talk about the past; it signals that the situation is unreal. Each pattern has a fixed set of tense choices, so learning the patterns is more effective than reasoning from meaning alone.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: For an if-sentence, ask: is the situation real (type 1), unreal now (type 2), or unreal in the past (type 3)? Then use the matching pair: present/will, past/would, past perfect/would have.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Conditionals
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Type 1: If + present, will + V1.  Type 2: If + past (were), would + V1.  Type 3: If + had + V3, would have + V3
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Pick the type by the reality of the situation.
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: If it rains, we will cancel; If I were rich, I would travel; If I had known, I would have told

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Reported speech
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Present → past; past → past perfect; will → would; tomorrow → the next day; yesterday → the previous day
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: "I am busy" → He said that he was busy

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Wish and would rather
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: I wish + past (present wish); I wish + had + V3 (past regret); would rather + subject + past
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: I wish I knew; I would rather you stayed

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Hardly/no sooner
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Hardly had + S + V3 + when …;  No sooner had + S + V3 + than …
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: No sooner had he left than it rained

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Completion by a time
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: By + future time → future perfect;  By the time + past → past perfect
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: By 2030 we will have completed the project

mainNarrative: Conditionals depend on how real the situation is. If it rains tomorrow, we will cancel the trip (real future: present + will). If I were rich, I would travel the world (unreal present: past + would; use were for all subjects). If she had worked harder, she would have passed (unreal past: past perfect + would have).

In reported speech, the verb moves one step back after a past reporting verb. "I am busy" becomes "He said that he was busy". "I will come tomorrow" becomes "He said that he would come the next day". Time words change too: yesterday becomes the previous day.

After wish, use a past form for an unreal present: I wish I knew the answer. Use the past perfect for a past regret: I wish I had known. After "would rather" with a different subject use the past: I would rather you stayed here tomorrow. After "it is high time", use the past: It is high time we left.

For sequences, hardly and no sooner take the past perfect and inversion: Hardly had he reached when it started to rain; No sooner had she left than it rained. Notice when after hardly and than after no sooner.

By + a future time takes the future perfect: By 2030 we will have completed the project. By the time you arrive, I will have cooked dinner. After verbs of suggestion, use the base form: He suggested that she see a doctor.

deepDiveAspects.title: Mixed conditionals
deepDiveAspects.content: A past cause with a present result: If I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor now. Use past perfect in the if-clause and would + base in the main clause.

deepDiveAspects.title: Were for all subjects
deepDiveAspects.content: In formal English, type 2 uses were for all subjects: If he were here. "Was" is common in speech but "were" is the exam answer.

solvedExamples.title: Conditionals
solvedExamples.question: Choose the correct form: "If I ___ the answer, I would have told you." (knew / had known / know / would know)
solvedExamples.conceptOrFormula: Type 3 uses past perfect in the if-clause.

steps.title: Identify the type
steps.explanation: "Would have told" signals an unreal past.

solvedExamples.title: Reported speech
solvedExamples.question: Report: He said, "I will come tomorrow."
solvedExamples.conceptOrFormula: Shift will → would, tomorrow → the next day.
solvedExamples.finalAnswer: He said that he would come the next day.
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The reporting verb is in the past.

solvedExamples.title: Hardly … when
solvedExamples.question: Complete: "Hardly ___ he reached the station when the train left." (has / had / did / was)
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The first action is completed before the second.

shortcutMethods.title: Pattern pairs

traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Memorise the pairs: present/will; past/would; past perfect/would have; hardly had … when; no sooner had … than; wish + past.

rulesForApplication: Reported speech shifts back one tense.

commonMistakes.howToAvoid: The if-clause never takes would in these types.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: Check which conditional the main clause shows and match the if-clause.

quickFormulas: If + had V3, would have V3

selfCheckQuestions: Can I complete a type 3 conditional?
